You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis

Details:
The failing test `testNotPositiveDefinite()` constructs a 5x5 matrix that is not positive definite and expects the Cholesky decomposition construction to throw a NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException. However, it appears that this exception was not thrown as expected.

The CholeskyDecompositionImpl constructor that accepts a RealMatrix checks for three conditions before performing the decomposition:
1) The matrix must be square.
2) The matrix must be symmetric within a relative threshold.
3) The matrix must be strictly positive definite with diagonal elements above an absolute threshold.

Inside the constructor (lines 93-151), the code first verifies the matrix is square, then copies the matrix data and checks the diagonal entries to ensure they are above the absolute positivity threshold (to guarantee positive definiteness). If any diagonal element is below this threshold, a NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException is thrown (line 115).

The code then verifies symmetry by comparing off-diagonal elements within a relative symmetry threshold. If the difference is too large, NotSymmetricMatrixException is thrown.

After these checks, the code performs the Cholesky decomposition (lines 131-149). The diagonal elements are square-rooted and used to update the trailing submatrix.

The problem is likely that the matrix in the test, although not positive definite in a mathematical sense, does not have any diagonal element less than the absolute positivity threshold at the start of the check (line 114). Because the positivity check is done only on diagonal entries before decomposition, the constructor misses negative definiteness caused by other eigenvalues or positive definiteness violations that don't show as negative or zero diagonal entries initially.

Since the constructor does not perform a full positive definiteness check and only screens diagonal elements with a threshold, some matrices that are not positive definite by definition may incorrectly pass this constructor check and result in a decomposition without throwing the expected exception.

Therefore, the cause of the test failure is that the CholeskyDecompositionImpl constructor incorrectly accepts certain non-positive definite matrices that have all diagonal elements above the threshold during the initial check. This discrepancy causes the NotPositiveDefiniteMatrixException to not be thrown in those cases.

No relevant clues were found in recent bug reports, and the test code clearly expects the exception. The faults are within the constructor of CholeskyDecompositionImpl where positive definiteness validation is incomplete.

This diagnosis matches the provided code and test behavior, explaining why the test fails to trigger the exception on the given matrix.

The key location to fix is the constructor CholeskyDecompositionImpl(RealMatrix, double, double), to improve the positive definite validation beyond the diagonal threshold check alone.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
